book: 008 - Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_

chapters.relation: Per Broman argues that Allen's debt to Ingmar Bergman is aesthetic recomposition rather than mere parody: Another Woman nearly remakes Wild Strawberries (Marion Post's road to self-knowledge mirrors Professor Borg's), while Deconstructing Harry so distorts the same honored-by-the-alma-mater plot (a prostitute, a kidnapped son, a Volvo, a detour to hell) that spotting the allusions becomes a rewarding puzzle. Casting Max von Sydow as the painter Frederick in Hannah and Her Sisters, and switching from jazz to Bach and Schubert at serious moments, imports the Bergmanesque world into Allen's Manhattan. Using Huyssen's modernism/postmodernism divide and Eco's account of postmodern irony, the chapter claims Allen's ironic allusions purge Bergman of pretension while claiming tradition's justification, and that for Allen's artist characters art is the mirror of life and the key to self-understanding rather than a carrier of metaphysical truth.

Sander Lee reads A Midsummer Night's Sex Comedy as Allen's warning against hedonism, tracing that ethos to empiricist thought from Hobbes and Locke through Bentham's utilitarianism to American pragmatism, embodied in Leopold Sturgis, an Ayer-style positivist philosopher who denies everything unprovable yet dies of passion with Dulcy and is deified by Andrew's spirit ball as pagan 'pure essence'. Using Sartre's Nausea, the chapter shows Andrew and Ariel's attempt to recreate their lost 'perfect moment' by the brook failing on every count, proving such moments inauthentic fantasies that ignore freedom, responsibility, and the passage of time. Through Bazin's Nietzschean reading of Renoir (Apollonian order versus Dionysian impulse), it argues that unlike Isaac Davis in Manhattan, the film's characters end more committed to hedonism than they began, with no character left qualified to condemn it.

David Detmer treats Zelig, the mock-documentary 'chameleon man' who turns black, Chinese, fat, or a Nazi depending on his company, as a stark dramatization of personal identity and the existentialist critique of inauthenticity. After rejecting the memory, bodily-continuity, and immaterial-soul criteria of identity, the chapter takes the existentialist line, quoting Heidegger on Dasein's selfhood, that a self is its choices, projects, and commitments, so Zelig's chameleonism is self-estrangement motivated by fear and the craving to be liked. Politically, the chapter draws Allen's lesson that genocides happen not because millions go mad but because millions passively conform, made literal by Zelig appearing at a Hitler rally, and supports it with Asch's conformity experiments and Milgram's obedience studies.

chapters.file: ch24 - The End Is It All Darkness.md
chapters.relation: John Pappas reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Glaucon's ring of Gyges in Plato's Republic: Judah Rosenthal's wealth and prestige are his invisibility ring, and when his mistress Dolores threatens exposure he 'pushes the button', has his gangster brother Jack murder her, and gets away with it. Against Socrates' claim that injustice corrodes the harmonious soul and that virtue is its own reward, the film, unlike Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment, lets the murderer and the 'yutz' Lester prosper while honest Clifford loses everything; Bergson's theory of the comic explains why Lester is invisible to himself, and Rousseau's reverie about what he would do with the ring marks Clifford as the one man who might use it decently. Aunt May's post-Holocaust atheism, 'might makes right' with nothing 'handed down in stone', supplies the argument from evil that releases Judah, leaving only the qualified hope that it is 'not all darkness'.

Jill Gordon reads Another Woman as a film about self-knowledge structured by Socrates' self-seeing eye from Plato's Alcibiades I: just as an eye sees itself only in another eye, the emotionally walled-off philosophy professor Marion Post finally sees her own repression by overhearing the 'other woman' Hope's therapy through a vent. Each of her relationships, with husband Ken, brother Paul, renounced lover Larry, stepdaughter Laura, and friend Claire, mirrors back truths ('she stands above people and evaluates them') that her self-deception refuses until her dream stages her own analysis and the final session describes her own life exactly. Counting the irrecoverable cost of her chances (Larry, the aborted child), the chapter closes with Rilke's 'Archaic Torso of Apollo', 'You must change your life', as the command Marion finally obeys, yielding a hard-won and still hopeful transformation.

Mary Nichols argues The Curse of the Jade Scorpion answers The Maltese Falcon: where Sam Spade's cynicism leaves society no reason to trust its lone hero, C.W. Briggs, unknowingly stealing for the magician Polgar while hypnotized, is saved by love, friendship, and the office community of North Coast Casualty. The jade scorpion's trance, meant to cover crime, uncovers truth, as C.W. and Betty Ann admit under hypnosis the love and fear their waking selves hide, so that 'crystal clear' memory and self-knowledge, rather than Spade's rejection of dreams, free them from both the curse and crime. Against the noir world and Lester's 'comedy is tragedy plus time', the chapter holds that everyone has 'a little bit of larceny' in them and that experiences of love, friendship, and community are what form the character that keeps it in check.

chapters.file: ch27 - Entertainment for Intellectuals A Woody Allen Filmography.md

holes.name: Postmodern Irony and the Great Divide
holes.what: The postmodern attitude (Eco, Huyssen) of consciously reworking the great models of high modernism with irony instead of naive sincerity, eroding the divide between high art and mass culture.
holes.why: Chapter 20 reads Allen's Bergman allusions in Another Woman and Deconstructing Harry as ironic 'recompositions' positioned between modernism and postmodernism via Huyssen's After the Great Divide and Eco's Barbara Cartland example, and no taxonomy slug covers allusion, irony, or the modernism/postmodernism debate in art.

holes.name: Logical Positivism (verifiability theory of meaning)
holes.what: The Vienna Circle/Ayer doctrine that only tautologies and empirically verifiable statements are meaningful, dismissing ethics, religion, and metaphysics as nonsense.
holes.why: Chapter 22 builds the character of Leopold Sturgis, the analytic philosopher whose empiricism underwrites the film's hedonism and whom Allen mocks, directly on Ayer's verifiability theory, which the taxonomy lacks despite having its critics.

holes.name: Laughter and the Comic (Bergson)
holes.what: Bergson's theory that the comic arises from 'the mechanical encrusted upon the living' and that the comic person is invisible to himself while remaining visible to the world.
holes.why: Chapter 24 applies Bergson's Laughter to explain why Lester in Crimes and Misdemeanors is a comic character incapable of seeing his own defect, a philosophy-of-humor tool absent from the taxonomy.
